title: Trump Raises Global Tariff to 15% After Supreme Court Ruling
description_short: Trump announced a 15% temporary global tariff under Section 122 after the Supreme Court struck down his prior program.
description_medium: On February 21, 2026, Donald Trump announced that the temporary global tariff would rise from 10% to 15% under Section 122, after the Supreme Court struck down his earlier tariff program. The announcement named a different legal authority for the new rate. Its effective date, product coverage and exemptions are not established here, so the practical reach of the increase remains unclear.
description_long: On February 21, 2026, Donald Trump announced that the temporary global tariff would rise from 10% to 15% under Section 122. He made the announcement after the Supreme Court struck down his earlier tariff program, invoking a different statutory authority for the new rate. The Court’s ruling concerned the prior program; the announcement described a separate step the administration intended to take afterward. The 15% figure identifies the announced rate, but by itself does not show when importers would begin paying it or which products would be covered. The details needed to assess the policy’s reach—its effective date, exemptions and implementation—are not established in the supplied facts. Nor do they show how much tariff revenue was collected or what the increase ultimately cost businesses and consumers. The sequence is clear: a court ruling against the earlier program was followed by a new tariff announcement. Its practical and legal consequences depend on details beyond the rate itself.

title: Trump Classified-Records Promise Marked Kept While Broader Transparency Disputes Persisted
description_short: Trump Classified-Records Promise Marked Kept While Broader Transparency Disputes Persisted
description_medium: AP's tracker listed Trump's promise to release key classified files as kept, but the broader information-governance landscape remained contested in parallel controversies. The contrast highlighted a recurring dynamic: a narrow tracked promise can score as complete while adjacent transparency issues continue to fuel institutional mistrust. Completion metrics and accountability confidence are not always the same thing.
description_long: The Associated Press’s promise tracker marked Donald Trump’s pledge to release key classified files as kept. The tracker’s status applies to that specific pledge; the files and the exact terms of the promise are not identified in the supplied account. A separate Washington Post report, published in April 2026, described changes to White House rules for preserving presidential records. One account concerns the reported completion of a disclosure promise, while the other concerns recordkeeping policy. The two reports do not establish that the same files were covered by the revised rules, that any promised files were lost or withheld, or that the policy change reversed the tracker’s assessment. A “kept” rating therefore should not be read as a judgment on every transparency practice. Likewise, a change to preservation rules alone does not prove a failure to release the files covered by the promise. The specific records, promise language and policy changes would need to be compared before the two developments could be connected.

title: Trump-Era Claims of Full Epstein Transparency Clashed With DOJ Webpage File Disappearances
description_short: Trump-Era Claims of Full Epstein Transparency Clashed With DOJ Webpage File Disappearances
description_medium: The Associated Press reported on December 20, 2025, that at least 16 files were no longer visible on the Justice Department webpage for Jeffrey Epstein-related documents. The reported count describes a change to the public page; it does not show that the underlying records were destroyed. AP did not identify each file or explain why it disappeared.
description_long: On December 20, 2025, the Associated Press reported that at least 16 files had disappeared from a Justice Department webpage containing documents related to Jeffrey Epstein. The count concerns files no longer visible to visitors on that page. It does not establish that the underlying government records were destroyed, removed from federal custody or withheld by a particular official. The report did not identify the files one by one, give a removal date for each, or explain who changed the page and why. A public promise of full disclosure would have to be matched against the specific documents and the language of that promise before the two could be compared. The reported absence raises a concrete question about public access, but it does not by itself prove a contradiction by Donald Trump or establish that the files were lost. The page’s version history and a Justice Department explanation would clarify whether the material was moved, corrected, restricted or removed.

title: Trump's Full-Disclosure Story Stayed Exposed to AP's Countable Gap

description_medium: On December 20, 2025, AP reported that at least 16 files had disappeared from the Justice Department’s online collection of Jeffrey Epstein-related records. That establishes a reported gap in what visitors could see on the webpage, not the destruction of the underlying files. The report did not say who removed them or why.
description_long: The Associated Press reported on December 20, 2025, that at least 16 files were missing from a Justice Department webpage devoted to Jeffrey Epstein-related documents. The report concerns public access to the online collection. A file disappearing from a webpage does not establish that the government destroyed its copy or removed it from official custody. The account did not name the affected files, give individual dates for their disappearance, or identify the person who changed the page. It also did not explain whether the files were moved, corrected or deliberately withheld. The number gives the reported change a concrete scale, but does not resolve its cause. To determine whether the incident contradicted a promise of full disclosure, readers would need to know which files the promise covered and whether they were later made available elsewhere. The report alone does not establish that Donald Trump directed the page change or that the underlying records were lost.

description_short: Trump: Right-wing website Breitbart is launched in Israel

description_long: Jewish Telegraphic Agency reporting dates Breitbart Jerusalem’s launch to November 2015. CEO Larry Solov recalled that he and founder Andrew Breitbart discussed creating a media company during a 2007 trip to Jerusalem; the trip preceded the launch by more than eight years. The two dates describe different events: an early conversation about a company and the later opening of an Israel-focused publication. The account also notes that Donald Trump appointed former Breitbart chair Stephen Bannon as chief strategist in November 2016. That later appointment connects Trump to a former Breitbart executive, but it does not show that Trump created or directed Breitbart Jerusalem. The January 2007 date in the title therefore conflates the Jerusalem trip with the site’s 2015 launch. The reported history supports describing the 2007 discussion, the 2015 publication launch and Bannon’s 2016 appointment as separate milestones. It does not establish the stronger claim that Trump was involved in launching the Israeli website.
